content: Strategies are required to address the challenges of linking individuals to care following HIV self-testing (HIVST) and community-based HIV testing services (HTS) when linkage rates are suboptimal. Some service delivery models demonstrate higher linkage rates than others. For instance, there is evidence, albeit of low quality, suggesting that combining HIVST with home-based antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and linkage escorts may improve linkage rates compared to facility-based ART initiation and self-referral. Community-based HTS has achieved high linkage rates in certain contexts. For example, HIV testing integrated with partner services resulted in a pooled linkage rate of 79%. A combination of models, such as mobile, outreach, and home-based testing, achieved pooled linkage rates of 78% for the general population and 85% for key populations. Stand-alone voluntary counseling and testing for key populations achieved a pooled linkage rate of 83%. However, some models and populations experienced lower linkage rates, such as home-based testing (51%), transgender individuals (41%), and people who inject drugs (44%). Additional support may be necessary to improve linkage in these contexts and populations. Provider-assisted referral, also known as assisted partner notification or index testing, is recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for all individuals diagnosed with HIV. This approach facilitates voluntary HIV testing for their sexual and/or drug-injecting partners. Counseling, while important, should be part of a broader evidence-based linkage strategy. Post-test counseling messages alone have minimal impact on linkage rates. Although individuals newly diagnosed with HIV may be motivated to change behaviors, counseling alone does not consistently lead to behavior change. In settings where linkage is suboptimal, additional evidence-based strategies can be considered, particularly for scaling up self-testing and community-based HTS, such as home-based and outreach models. Peer and community support, including patient navigators and linkage escorts, is recommended by WHO to facilitate linkage. Evidence suggests that patient navigators can improve linkage to care. Peer-led support, including support from individuals living with HIV, can also enhance linkage. For example, a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Zambia among young people aged 15–24 who self-tested found that patient escorts nearly tripled linkage to ART compared to self-referral cards. In Eswatini, peer-based case management using patient navigators, weekly phone calls, reminders, and follow-up counseling resulted in 96% of individuals initiating ART during the study period. Home-based ART initiation following home-based HTS or other outreach approaches can achieve high linkage rates. An RCT in Lesotho reported a 13% higher linkage rate and a 16% increase in viral suppression with home-based HTS and same-day home-based ART initiation compared to home-based HTS with referral for facility-based ART initiation. Similarly, an RCT in Malawi found that home-based HIVST distribution and ART initiation led to a threefold higher linkage rate compared to home-based HIVST distribution with standard facility-based ART initiation. The use of incentives, including financial incentives, has shown mixed results in improving linkage. A recent review found that offering economic incentives in settings with treat all policies did not increase linkage or ART initiation. WHO's systematic review indicates limited and highly variable evidence on the impact of incentives on linkage to prevention, treatment, and care. While incentives may slightly improve HTS uptake, they do not appear to significantly affect ART initiation or viral suppression rates. Flexible, inclusive, non-judgmental, and cost-free services are essential to support linkage and rapid ART initiation. Structural, legal, and policy barriers, as well as fear of criminalization and prosecution, can negatively impact linkage, particularly among key populations, adolescents, and young people. Programs must work to create a supportive environment that enables individuals living with HIV to access care and treatment. Digital health tools, including social media, videos, text messaging, and other applications, show promise in facilitating linkage. Evidence suggests that videos can increase HTS uptake, although their impact on linkage is uncertain, and they may be costly. Further research is needed to explore how digital platforms, particularly social media and web-based tools, can be adapted to support linkage and rapid ART initiation at an affordable cost. Strategies to re-link individuals who have previously disengaged from care or declined ART are limited, and further research is needed in this area. Countries should review their national guidelines and consider incorporating clear linkage strategies and policies, including specific approaches, interventions, and designated roles to support linkage and rapid ART initiation. Monitoring the effectiveness of these strategies is essential. Given the declining number of individuals unaware of their HIV status in many countries, most people undergoing HIV testing are likely to be HIV-negative. To maximize program impact and cost-effectiveness, it is crucial to optimize service delivery to reach HIV-negative individuals at ongoing risk and link them to effective prevention interventions. HTS should prioritize and facilitate linkage to prevention for these individuals. Once engaged in prevention interventions, HTS can serve as part of prevention monitoring, such as quarterly testing for individuals on pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), to identify new infections and initiate ART promptly.
